clue.text: Drunkard catches cold — check what he's on?

indicators.note: catching something is taking hold of it, so the drunkard word takes the cold letter inside

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
ch is the chess notation for check

explanation.surface: A boozer has come down with a chill, so somebody ought to look at what he has been taking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catches' puts C inside SOT. 'check' looks like an instruction to investigate but is the chess abbreviation CH. The question mark admits that whisky is only one thing a drunkard might be on.
explanation.definitionFit: A drunkard is 'on' some drink, and whisky from Scotland is a likely example.

clue.text: Progress round town that could be done by halves?

definitions.text: Progress round town that could be done by halves?

parts.words: Progress round town that could be done by halves?
parts.note: halves are half-pints of beer in Britain, so this is a tour of a town's bars taken one small glass at a time

explanation.definitionFit: A drinking tour from bar to bar is a journey around town, and ordering half-pints is one way to last the course.

clue.text: Have a sociable night out committing assaults?

definitions.meaning: to spend the evening dancing at nightspots
whimsically, to set off hitting people with a heavy stick

explanation.surface: An evening with friends that somehow involves attacking people.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: an evening of dancing at nightspots, and, fancifully, setting out to beat people with cudgels.

clue.text: Empty one in front

indicators.note: in places the letter for one inside the word for front

parts.note: the van is the front of an advancing army, short for vanguard
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The person at the head of the queue has nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms in the sense of hollow or worthless, as in empty promises.

clue.text: Horse: ahead of time, reining it back in with enthusiasm

parts.note: H is a slang abbreviation for horse, meaning heroin

indicators.note: reining something in holds it back within bounds, so the word for ahead of time holds the turned pair inside

parts.note: early means ahead of time

indicators.note: back tells you the word it is written right to left

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rider on a horse running ahead of schedule eagerly pulls it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reining' and the later 'in' work together as the container signal, and 'back' turns 'it' to TI before it goes inside. 'Horse' is slang for heroin, hence its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb for doing something with gusto, as in laughing or eating with vigour.

clue.text: Followed honour — you finally ducked

parts.note: the OBE, Officer of the Order of the British Empire, is a British honour
ye is an old word for you

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of the word after it

explanation.surface: Someone pursued an award, and in the end you dodged out of the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the last letter of 'ducked'. OBE is a British honour awarded by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow orders is to comply with them, the same past tense.

clue.text: In the centre of a motorway, one heading for Dover

parts.note: M is the prefix for British motorways, as in the M1
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: heading for takes the head, the opening letter, of the next word

explanation.surface: A lone driver in the middle of a major road, bound for the Channel port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading for' takes the first letter of Dover. British motorways are numbered with an M, and M plus one gives the M1.
explanation.definitionFit: A preposition meaning surrounded by or among.

clue.text: Hear what eg Pavarotti could reach, in the main

indicators.note: hear tells you to listen to the phrase rather than read its spelling

parts.note: the tenor Pavarotti was famous for hitting high Cs, the top notes of his range

explanation.surface: Listen to the heights a great tenor could hit, for the most part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' makes it a soundalike: the tenor's top notes, high Cs, give the answer when spoken. 'in the main' reads as 'mostly', but the main is the open ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is an old word for the open ocean, as in the Spanish Main.

clue.text: There's a lot to conceal a pig in wood

indicators.note: concealing something is hiding it within, so the word for a lot wraps round the rest

parts.note: many means a lot
a hog is a pig

explanation.surface: A forest has plenty of space where a pig could be hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to conceal' is the container signal. 'wood' reads as a forest where an animal might hide, but it is timber.
explanation.definitionFit: An example of a timber, a reddish-brown tropical hardwood used for furniture.

clue.text: Turn to rip front off malicious poster

indicators.note: ripping the front off a word tears away its opening letter

parts.note: a troll is someone who posts malicious messages online

explanation.surface: Someone takes their go at tearing the top off a nasty placard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to rip front off' removes the T from TROLL. The poster looks like a placard but is a person posting online.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as verbs: to rotate or revolve, as a wheel does.

clue.text: Journalist's breaking news about monarchy

indicators.note: breaking into something is forcing a way inside, so the journalist goes within the other word
about turns the word news to face the other way

parts.note: taken as written
ed, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter has a hot scoop concerning the royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking news' reads as one phrase but splits between two instructions: 'about' turns the word to SWEN, and 'breaking' sends the journalist inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: the Scandinavian country is a kingdom with a king as head of state.

clue.text: Is united, never sundered, that's all

indicators.note: something sundered is broken apart, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names
taken as written

explanation.surface: A declaration of unbreakable togetherness, and nothing more to say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'never sundered' reads as one phrase, but 'sundered' is the anagram signal acting on ISUNEVER. 'that's' merely links to the one-word definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cosmos is everything that exists, the totality of things.

clue.text: EastEnders' burglar, and the area he controls?

indicators.note: people from London's East End, Cockneys, traditionally say th as f, so the word is given as they would pronounce it

parts.note: a burglar is a thief

explanation.surface: A housebreaker from a London soap opera, and the patch he runs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'EastEnders'' signals Cockney pronunciation, where th becomes f, so THIEF is said with an F. EastEnders is also a British TV soap set in east London.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain or territory under one person's control, originally a feudal estate.

clue.text: Relatively important dictator?

parts.note: relatively hints at a family relation: a sibling who is senior, sharing a name with the all-seeing tyrant of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four

explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's all-watching ruler in Nineteen Eighty-Four is a tyrant, and his name is an older male sibling, a relation of some importance.

clue.text: Ass welcomes extremely elegant turncoat

indicators.note: welcoming someone is taking them in, so the animal word takes the pair of letters inside

parts.note: an ass is an animal that brays, whimsically a brayer

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the next word, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A fool greets a very stylish defector.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcomes' is the container signal and 'extremely' takes the first and last letters of its neighbour. Calling a donkey by the noise it makes is a crossword whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms for a traitor, someone who switches sides and sells out their own.

clue.text: Holofernes for one gets nothing out of faulty notepad

indicators.note: something faulty is not in working order, so the letters are put into a different order
out of says the letter for nothing is taken away from the word

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A character gets no use from a broken jotter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' takes the O from NOTEPAD and 'faulty' rearranges the remaining NTEPAD. Holofernes is the fussy schoolmaster in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's schoolmaster in Love's Labour's Lost is a classic example of a fussy stickler for learning.

clue.text: Old woman tucking right into ice cream

indicators.note: tucking a letter into a word places it inside

parts.note: a cone is an ice cream served in a wafer cornet

explanation.surface: An elderly lady eagerly eating a frozen dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking ... into' puts R inside CONE. 'tucking right into' reads as eating heartily.
explanation.definitionFit: A withered elderly female, a hag.

clue.text: No music channel wants short story, one gloomy over love

indicators.note: short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a tale is a story

indicators.note: over turns the two pieces as one run, read from the end

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
dark means gloomy
love is a score of zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A station without songs is after a brief tale about a morose person getting past a romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' drops the E of TALE; 'over' turns IDARK into KRADI.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcasting station devoted to speech and phone-ins plays no songs.

clue.text: Bases planted around state in arrogance

indicators.note: planted around sets the first word on either side of the state

parts.note: hubs are centres of operation, bases
RI is the abbreviation for Rhode Island, a US state

explanation.surface: Military camps set up all over a country out of sheer pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'planted around' is the container signal. 'state' suggests a country hosting army camps, but it is an American one, Rhode Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms for overweening pride.

clue.text: After editing, prune only eighty letters from him

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for a man's name, here a Roman author famous for his correspondence

indicators.note: editing text reworks it, so the three words are reworked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An editor cuts a man's correspondence down to just eighty items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After editing' rearranges PRUNEONLYEIGHTY. The Roman writer is remembered chiefly for his letters, including the eyewitness account of Vesuvius erupting, so 'letters from him' points at the man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman author and lawyer is best known for his published correspondence, so he is the man the letters come from.

clue.text: My word, how Ira's lyrics were set

definitions.meaning: Ira Gershwin's words were put to music composed by his brother, whose first name completes the phrase

explanation.surface: An exclamation about the way a lyricist's words were put to music.
explanation.definitionFit: Both an old-fashioned exclamation of surprise and a statement of which Gershwin composed the tunes.

clue.text: Show criticism, outspoken

indicators.note: outspoken, taken literally as spoken out, says the word is to be said rather than spelt

parts.note: a review is a piece of criticism

explanation.surface: Someone displays frank disapproval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outspoken' is the soundalike signal: REVIEW is pronounced the same. 'Show' reads as a verb but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical entertainment of sketches and songs.

clue.text: For administrators, what can divide a little from the lot

parts.note: a whit is a tiny amount, as in not a whit
eh? is what you say when you want something repeated, like what?
all means the lot, everything

explanation.surface: Officials want the thing that separates a small share from everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can divide ... from' tells you the word for 'what' stands between the other two. The answer is a London street of government ministries, used as a name for the British civil service.
explanation.definitionFit: The London street housing government ministries is shorthand for Britain's civil servants.

clue.text: Shabby trick takes in husband for the time being

parts.note: mean and shabby both describe poor, ungenerous behaviour

indicators.note: taking something in is receiving it inside, so the trick word holds the letter

parts.note: a wile is a cunning trick
H is the genealogical abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A low con fools a married man for now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes in' puts H inside WILE. 'Shabby trick' reads as one phrase but is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbial phrases for in the interim.

clue.text: Overate? Might have refused it, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters could be otherwise, in another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone ate too much and could have turned the food down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges REFUSEDIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To have indulged to excess, fed until overfull.

clue.text: A number of Irish names retained by boarder? No!

indicators.note: retained by says the letters are kept inside the other word

parts.note: a day boy is a pupil at a boarding school who goes home at night, so not a boarder
N is the abbreviation for name, so two names are NN

explanation.surface: Several Irish surnames are kept by a lodger, or perhaps not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retained by' is the container signal. 'boarder? No!' is a pupil at a British boarding school who lives at home, and 'number' is a song, not a quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous Irish ballad sung to the Londonderry Air; number here is a song.

clue.text: Military evaluation that is fresh one's rejected

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the two pieces are read as one run from the end

parts.note: pert and fresh both mean cheeky
one is I, and with the possessive that gives IS

explanation.surface: An army assessment says a new recruit has been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns PERTIS round. The answer is army shorthand for a situation report.
explanation.definitionFit: Army shorthand for a situation report, an assessment of how things stand.

clue.text: Following opening does perhaps delay

indicators.note: opening something is splitting it apart, so the letter goes inside the animal word

parts.note: does are female deer, one example of them
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: After the launch, something may well hold things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' puts F inside DEER. 'does' reads as the verb but is the plural of doe.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as verbs: to postpone or put off.

clue.text: Wooster never holds back

indicators.note: holds says the two words contain the answer in consecutive letters

explanation.surface: Bertie Wooster always charges ahead without restraint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' marks the run of letters spanning the two words. 'holds back' reads as one phrase, but 'back' alone is the rear of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear end of a ship.
